scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.

Imported coverage is 1600 to 1815, roughly east-central Northern Territory. The card is about Antekerrepenh people and the language, not a historical state. Later sources do not authenticate the imported dates or polygon.

The language profile and AIATSIS identifiers align Antekerrepenh with Andegerebenha, C12. Similar-looking names for Antakirinja or other peoples are not treated as interchangeable. The Pedirka regional assessment’s broad name list is not used to relocate this destination.

Roth’s Undekerebina name is linked with Antekerrepenh in the AUSTLANG-derived profile and in linguistic bibliographies. His 1897 text has a colonial perspective and racist language, which the narrative does not reproduce or endorse.

Roth’s book was read through the Cornell scan at https://cdstar.eva.mpg.de/bitstreams/EAEA0-128F-B2EC-A3B7-0/1897_Roth_Ethnological_studies.pdf . Printed pages 80, 104 and 135 were rendered and inspected. The public-domain status is recorded at https://wellcomecollection.org/works/z74yavfk .

The grindstone discussion is regional manufacture and trade, not an archaeological discovery with an identified maker. No chronology of first invention or universal ethnic attribution is inferred. Cordage and fruit signs are the specific group-attributed descriptions in section 86.
The 1890s period is an approximate bracket around the 1897 publication, not an asserted founding or extinction date. Goods and routes are attributed to Roth’s account.

AIATSIS public finding aids were read; the audio was not listened to, copied or republished. Entries describe catalogue evidence and name speakers without supplying lyrics, ritual explanations or unverified transcriptions.

BREEN_G12-001882A changes from Antekerrepenh to Pitta Pitta; BREEN_G13-001886A changes to Warluwarra. Attribution follows the timed sections, not a whole-reel language label. BREEN_G13 has a 1978 date inconsistent with its 1970 title for some earlier items; those items and dates are not used.

Breen’s kinship survey is a heritage work published in 2022, based on earlier fieldwork. Its descriptions of remembered language are not used as a current census or evidence that the people have disappeared.
The JCU acknowledgement supports continuing recognition of country and the named people, not a verified native-title judgment, population count or language-revival outcome.
Detailed housing construction, an archaeological sequence and a specific loss-of-sovereignty event were not established by the checked evidence. No speculative conqueror or successor link is added.
Independent historical review, identity and border verification, and depth certification remain pending.
